verdicts.why: Whether `tableIn.available() > 0` (line 148) / `arrayIn.available() > 0` (line 244) can terminate early depends entirely on TruncatedInputStream.available(), and TruncatedInputStream.java is not among the provided files; nothing in ValueReader.java decides it.

A -SNAPSHOT trunk version is the normal development state and the pom configures maven-release-plugin (line 737) to stamp the release version; the claim's core assertion that "each build may pull different code" is factually false because every dependency and plugin version in the pom is pinned (grep finds no version ranges, no LATEST/RELEASE, and no SNAPSHOT dependency).

groovy-all 2.4.21 is declared only as a plugin dependency of groovy-maven-plugin (pom.xml:597-603) that runs codegen at generate-sources from the project's own script and JSON spec, so it never ships in the artifact and no attacker supplies its input; "would affect all downstream builds" is wrong since consumers of amqp-client never execute it, and a 21st patch release of the 2.4 line contradicts the claimed 2016/2017 dates.

readBytes allocates `new byte[(int)contentLength]` (line 88) from a peer-supplied 32-bit length before `in.readFully` reads anything, and the only guard (line 87) still permits ~2 GB, so a few bytes of hostile framing can force a huge allocation; only the aside about table/array payloads is inaccurate (readTable/readArray do not call readBytes).

jetty-servlet is declared `<scope>test</scope>` (pom.xml:454-457) so it is never on a consumer's classpath and no attacker reaches it, and the version string 9.4.58.v20250814 is itself an August-2025 patch build, contradicting "reached end-of-life" with no security fixes.

The evidence asserts "No bounds checking is performed on contentLength before allocation", but line 87 is exactly that check, sitting between the read (line 86) and the allocation (line 88); the trigger value the claim names, contentLength equal to Integer.MAX_VALUE, is rejected by that check and throws UnsupportedOperationException (lines 92-93) instead of allocating.

The timestamp at line 269 is a plain data field wholly chosen by the same peer, so overflowing `readLong()*1000` gives an attacker no value they could not have sent directly as a normal timestamp; no bound is bypassed and no integrity property is crossed, so this is a robustness nit rather than a defect with impact.

Same as the other line-269 variants: a peer that can choose the 8-byte timestamp can already produce any Date it wants, so wrapping the multiplication yields no capability gain; the AMQP timestamp field is decoded data, not a security decision made by this library.

No attacker gain at line 269 (the sender already controls the timestamp value outright), and the named consequences are wrong for this code: message expiry in AMQP rides the `expiration` property handled by the broker, not this Date, and ValueReader makes no authorization decision.

The quoted code is verbatim: line 87's `contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE` admits nearly 2^31 bytes and line 88 allocates that array before line 89 reads any payload, so a tiny hostile length prefix forces the ~2.1 GB allocation the claim describes.

The stated overflow threshold is wrong by a factor of 1000 (Long.MAX_VALUE/1000 is ~9.223e15, not the 9,223,372,036,854 given), and in any case the peer that supplies the long at line 269 already controls the resulting Date, so no attacker capability is added.

Line 217 throws MalformedFrameException and aborts parsing, so nothing is silent and no type is corrupted; wanting the offending byte in the message text is a diagnostics/log-wording preference with no attacker capability and no information disclosed.

Every cited edge is real and correctly located: readFieldValue (158) -> readTable (181) -> readFieldValue (150) and readFieldValue -> readArray (184) -> readFieldValue (245), with no depth counter anywhere in the file and each nesting level costing only ~5-6 payload bytes.

Line 173 allocates a fixed `new byte[4]`, so the BigInteger at line 175 is always at most 32 bits and no attacker-controlled length exists; the claim concedes this and rests on a hypothetical "if this pattern were used elsewhere", which is not a defect in this code.

The recursion cycle it names is exactly what the file contains (readFieldValue 158-221, readTable 139-155 calling back at 150, readArray 237-249 calling back at 245) and no method in the file tracks or limits nesting depth.

Accurately describes line 87 as permitting up to Integer.MAX_VALUE-1 bytes and line 88 as allocating that array ahead of the readFully at line 89, so the length prefix alone (not the delivered bytes) drives heap consumption.

All four call sites cited (150, 158, 181, 184, 237, 245) match the file and the mutual recursion readTable/readFieldValue/readArray carries no depth limit; the nested TruncatedInputStream at line 146 bounds bytes, never stack frames.

The quoted snippets match lines 139-155 and 180-185 and there is no recursion guard, so a nested payload of a few tens of kilobytes reaches thousands of frames; only the term "StackOverflowException" is loose (Java throws StackOverflowError).

A GPG key id is the public identifier of a public key and is embedded in every signature the project has ever published, so `<gpg.keyname>` at pom.xml:124 discloses nothing; forging a release requires the private key, which the id does not provide, making the stated impact false.

`new String(b, "utf-8")` at line 70 is specified to replace malformed input with U+FFFD rather than throw or execute anything, and the length is capped at 255 bytes by readUnsignedByte at line 68; the claim identifies no capability an attacker gains, since header names and routing keys are attacker-chosen data whether or not the encoding is validated.

The described cycle is present verbatim (case 'F' at 181 -> readTable -> readFieldValue at 150; case 'A' at 184 -> readArray -> readFieldValue at 245) with no depth accounting, and readFieldValue is reached from the public readTable() at line 252, so peer-supplied frames drive it.

Correctly reads lines 86-94: the guard admits any length below Integer.MAX_VALUE and line 88 commits the allocation before a single payload byte is read, so a declared ~2 GB length is enough to trigger OutOfMemoryError.

Line 70 uses String(byte[], String), which is not deprecated in Java; it throws the checked UnsupportedEncodingException (not IllegalCharsetNameException/UnsupportedCharsetException) and never silently falls back to the platform default, so every factual premise of the claim is wrong.

Line 269 decodes a value the sending peer already controls end to end, so a wrapped Date is indistinguishable from the peer simply sending that Date; no guard is bypassed and the claim states no impact beyond "incorrect timestamp", which is the sender's prerogative anyway.

Internally inconsistent and non-exploitable: version 2.4.21 cannot postdate a 2015 end-of-life, and groovy-all is scoped to the groovy-maven-plugin's codegen execution (pom.xml:597-603) driven by the repo's own generate_amqp_sources.groovy and JSON spec, so there is no untrusted input and nothing reaches the published jar.

slf4j-api (pom.xml:376-378) is a logging facade compile dependency and the claim names no vulnerability, no attacker and no reachable impact - only a generic "EOL, upgrade" preference; for a library the declared slf4j-api version is a floor consumers can override, so nothing here is a defect.
